title: The Yellow Wall-Paper and The Giant Wistaria
author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
written: The Yellow Wall-Paper in two days at Pasadena in June 1890; The Giant Wistaria a little earlier
setting: A colonial mansion rented for the summer, and one upstairs room with barred windows, a nailed-down bed and paper the narrator is told not to mind
lengthNote: Two short stories: about 6,000 words and 3,000 words, the first told in undated journal entries that get shorter as they go
openingLine: It is very seldom that mere ordinary people like John and myself secure ancestral halls for the summer.
summary: A woman is brought to a rented country house to recover from what her husband, a physician, calls a slight hysterical tendency. She is forbidden to work or write, put in a top-floor room with barred windows, and left with nothing to look at but the wallpaper. She looks at it. What begins as irritation becomes study, then a pattern, then a figure behind the pattern, then a plan. The companion story in this volume, The Giant Wistaria, puts a second silenced woman in a second old house and lets a party of summer tenants find what is left of her.
referenceStyle: journal entry, identified by the phase of the story, not by page

sourceText.label: Project Gutenberg text of The Yellow Wallpaper (eBook 1952)
sourceText.note: The Astor edition follows the New England Magazine printing of January 1892 and records where later texts differ. This transcription of a later American printing is used for checking quotations; it spells the title word without a hyphen and prints repellant for repellent. The Giant Wistaria is not in it, so the quotations here are all from The Yellow Wall-Paper.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: In Pasadena, three years after Gilman had been treated with S. Weir Mitchell's rest cure and two years after she left her marriage.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: In The New England Magazine, which had printed The Giant Wistaria seven months earlier.

atAGlance.label: Form
atAGlance.note: Entries written in secret, in a house where writing is forbidden. The gaps between them are part of the story.

atAGlance.label: Length
atAGlance.note: Short enough to read at a sitting, which is how the accelerating entries are meant to be taken.

structure.label: The house
structure.title: A rented mansion, and a diagnosis
structure.summary: The narrator arrives at a house she likes and distrusts, with a husband who has decided what is wrong with her and what she may do about it. The rules are set out early: no work, no writing, phosphates, air, and the top-floor room, not the pretty one downstairs. Everything the story will need is established before anything happens.

scenes.title: Ancestral halls
scenes.summary: Delight in the house, a joke about ghosts, and the first admission that something is wrong that nobody will name.

scenes.title: Temporary nervous depression
scenes.summary: Her husband and her brother, both physicians of high standing, agree there is nothing much the matter. The story's central problem is that she half agrees with them.

scenes.title: Barred windows, a nailed bed
scenes.summary: She wanted the downstairs room with roses at the window; she is given the old nursery at the top of the house, with rings in the wall and a gate at the stairs.

structure.label: The pattern
structure.title: Studying the wallpaper
structure.summary: Deprived of company and of writing, she gives the paper the attention she would have given a book. The description sharpens as her boredom deepens: colour, then smell, then a sub-pattern visible only in certain light. Reading the wall is the only intellectual work she is allowed to do, and she does it well.

scenes.title: Repellant, almost revolting
scenes.summary: The yellow is described with a precision nobody in the house will listen to. Her eye is exact; her authority is nil.

scenes.title: John laughs at me
scenes.summary: Affection and dismissal arrive in the same sentences, which is what makes the marriage hard to argue with.

scenes.title: By moonlight it becomes bars
scenes.summary: The sub-pattern resolves. What she sees at night is a cage, and something inside it.

structure.label: The figure
structure.title: The woman behind the paper
structure.summary: The figure becomes a woman, then women, then a woman who creeps outside in daylight. The journal entries shorten and speed up, secrecy grows — she hides the writing, then hides her interest in the paper — and Jennie and John are recast as rivals who want the paper for themselves.

scenes.title: The woman behind shakes it
scenes.summary: The narrator stops describing a design and starts describing an act. The front pattern moves because someone is trying to get through it.

scenes.title: Creeping women
scenes.summary: She sees the woman outside, on the road and in the arbours, and says she always locks the door when she creeps by daylight herself.

scenes.title: They are watching it too
scenes.summary: John and Jennie are found looking at the paper. The narrator resolves that nobody else shall find it out.

structure.label: The last day
structure.title: Tearing down the paper
structure.summary: On the last day of the tenancy she locks herself in, throws the key into the path and strips the room. The final entries are almost without hesitation: the voice that has apologised for itself throughout announces that it has got out. John faints on the threshold, and she creeps over him.

scenes.title: All around the room
scenes.summary: She peels what she can reach and rages at what she cannot, having first made sure the door is locked and the rope is ready.

scenes.title: I've got out at last
scenes.summary: The sentence that has divided readers for a century: an escape, a breakdown, or both — and the name Jane, which appears nowhere else in the story.

scenes.title: Creeping over him
scenes.summary: The doctor faints in the doorway, the patient keeps moving, and the story ends on the floor.

structure.label: The Giant Wistaria
structure.title: The companion story, seven months earlier
structure.summary: A colonial family disposes of a daughter's disgrace and sails for England; a century later a party of summer tenants rent the abandoned house, joke about ghosts, and find a body beneath the wistaria root and a small skeleton in the well. The pairing is the point: the same silencing, told once from inside the room and once from the future, after everyone has stopped listening.

scenes.title: The family leaves
scenes.summary: A father, a mother and an unnamed daughter, whose child is not to be spoken of, sail for England and leave the house shut up.

scenes.title: A ghost story for the summer
scenes.summary: The new party competes to invent the house's history, which is the story's joke: they narrate over the woman whose remains are under them.

scenes.title: Under the root, in the well
scenes.summary: The evidence arrives without commentary. The story stops as soon as it is found, and leaves the tenants' cheerful theories standing.

characters.name: The narrator
characters.role: A young wife and new mother, under treatment in her husband's care
characters.summary: Observant, funny in the early entries, and systematically disbelieved. She is a good reader — her account of the paper is the most precise description in the story — and every skill she has is turned on the only object she is allowed. She is never named, unless Jane in the last line is her.
characters.clue: Writes in secret because writing is forbidden, and calls the journal dead paper and a great relief to her mind.

characters.name: John
characters.role: Her husband, a physician of high standing
characters.summary: Kind in his own account and immovable in practice. He laughs, calls her a blessed little goose, carries her upstairs, schedules her hours and will not hear of a change of room. Nothing he does is cruel by the standards he holds, which is the story's argument: the harm is in the standards.
characters.clue: Faints at the sight of what his treatment has produced, and is stepped over.

relationships.label: brother of, employer of the household

characters.name: Jennie
characters.summary: A perfect housekeeper who hopes for no better profession, and the narrator's warder by default. She is not unkind; she simply belongs to the arrangement. When she is found studying the paper, the narrator treats her as a competitor, not an ally, which is what the isolation has done.
characters.clue: Caught with her hand on the wallpaper, and afterwards told that the narrator can read it better alone.

characters.name: The woman in the paper
characters.role: The figure behind the front pattern
characters.summary: First a shape, then a woman stooping and creeping, then many women, then one who gets out into the garden by daylight. Whether she is a hallucination, a self-portrait or the story's one honest witness is the question every reading has to answer.
characters.clue: Shakes the bars from the inside; is last seen creeping outside, fast, in the open.

relationships.label: seen by, released by, merged with

characters.name: The baby
characters.role: The narrator's child, kept downstairs with Mary
characters.summary: Mentioned rarely and always with relief that someone else has charge of him. The relief is the most painful thing in the story: she cannot be with her child, cannot say so plainly, and is grateful for a separation she never chose.
characters.clue: She is glad his case is not hers, and cannot be with him without getting nervous.

characters.name: Weir Mitchell
characters.role: The physician named in the story, and the one who treated Gilman
characters.summary: He appears only as a threat: if she does not improve, John will send her to him in the autumn. Naming a living, famous doctor inside a piece of fiction was the story’s sharpest move, and the reason its first readers took it as an accusation, not a ghost story.
characters.clue: A name used to end an argument, invoked but never met.

themes.name: The rest cure
themes.summary: Rest is prescribed and enforced: a top-floor nursery with barred windows, a bed that will not move, a gate at the stairs and a schedule for every hour. The cure and the imprisonment are the same arrangement, described by the patient in the tone of someone being looked after.
themes.development: She asks for the downstairs room and is refused; she asks to go home and is refused; by the last day she has locked the door herself and thrown the key into the path, which is the first time confinement is her own decision.

themes.name: Medicine
themes.summary: Her husband is her doctor, her brother is a doctor, and the specialist is held in reserve as a threat. Disagreement is reclassified as a symptom, so there is no position from which she can be believed.
themes.development: The story opens with her half-accepting the diagnosis and ends with the doctor unconscious in the doorway — the only way the narrative can get him to stop talking.

themes.name: Work
themes.summary: She believes congenial work would do her good and is not allowed any. The story is unusually specific about what the ban costs: company, air, occupation and the right to write down what is happening to her.
themes.development: Writing goes underground in the first entries, becomes exhausting by the middle, and is replaced by the only intellectual task the room offers — reading the paper.

themes.name: Speech and silence
themes.summary: Every complaint has to be softened, and the softening is audible. She calls herself unreasonably angry, blames her nervousness, praises John's care and then records the facts that contradict it, leaving the reader to do the arithmetic.
themes.development: The apologetic manner thins as the entries shorten, and disappears entirely in the last two pages, where the sentences are short, declarative and unhedged.

themes.name: The unreliable journal
themes.summary: Everything comes through one voice, written in secret, in gaps between visits. The form supplies both the intimacy and the doubt: there is no outside account of the room, the paper or the woman in it.
themes.development: Early entries are dated by events and hedged with qualifications; later ones lose their frame, until the final pages are written in the present tense with the door locked.

themes.name: Secrecy
themes.summary: The journal is hidden, the interest in the paper is hidden, and by the end the discovery is hoarded like property. Secrecy starts as self-defence and becomes the shape of her thinking.
themes.development: She hides the writing from John, then hides the paper from Jennie, then locks the door and refuses to admit anyone — protecting a secret that has become the only thing that is hers.

themes.name: Escape
themes.summary: The figure in the paper begins as an object of study and ends as a first person. The last entries move from watching a woman creep to reporting her own creeping without marking the join.
themes.development: The name Jane in the final speech has no other use in the story; whether she has escaped her keepers, her role or herself is the question the ending deliberately leaves open.

techniques.name: The secret journal
techniques.definition: A first-person narrative written in entries, in the present tense, with gaps the reader must fill.
techniques.inThisBook: The form does the work an omniscient narrator would otherwise do. Entries stop when she is watched and resume when she is alone, so the silences mark the surveillance; and because writing is forbidden, the existence of the text is itself an act of disobedience.

techniques.name: Unreliable narrator
techniques.definition: A first-person account the reader has reason to doubt, with no corroborating voice in the text.
techniques.inThisBook: The doubt is unusually double-edged: she is wrong about the paper and right about the marriage. Readers who dismiss her testimony end up agreeing with John, which is the trap the story sets.

techniques.name: Symbolic objects
techniques.definition: Ordinary objects that accumulate meaning by repetition, without explanation.
techniques.inThisBook: The nailed-down bed, the barred windows, the gate at the stairs and the rings in the wall are introduced as the fittings of a nursery and are never glossed. The story lets the reader notice that they are also the fittings of a cell.

techniques.name: Gothic conventions
techniques.definition: Old house, isolated setting, a locked room and a figure that may or may not be there.
techniques.inThisBook: Every gothic expectation is raised and then declined: the house is not haunted, the ghost is wallpaper, and the horror is a medical arrangement everybody in the story considers reasonable. The Giant Wistaria supplies the conventional version for comparison.

techniques.name: Doors and windows
techniques.definition: Boundaries that mark who may pass and who may not.
techniques.inThisBook: She is carried up the stairs, kept behind a gate, and looks out of barred windows at a garden she is not in. The last scene puts the doctor across the doorway and makes her get past him on the floor.

techniques.name: Irony
techniques.definition: Saying one thing in terms that let the reader hear another.
techniques.inThisBook: He is very careful and loving, and hardly lets me stir without special direction — the sentence means both things, and the story is made of sentences like it.

techniques.name: Omission
techniques.definition: Gaps in the telling that the reader has to bridge.
techniques.inThisBook: Nothing is said about the birth, little about the baby, and the worst days are represented by their absence from the journal. The most important events in the story are the ones no entry covers.

quotations.text: It is very seldom that mere ordinary people like John and myself secure ancestral halls for the summer.
quotations.context: The opening sentence of the journal.
quotations.analysis: It is a social joke, told by someone pleased with her luck. It establishes the voice the story will use throughout — light, self-deprecating, interested in appearances — and the gothic set-up is delivered as a piece of good fortune, not a warning.

quotations.text: John is a physician, and perhaps—(I would not say it to a living soul, of course, but this is dead paper and a great relief to my mind)—perhaps that is one reason I do not get well faster.
quotations.context: A few lines into the journal, explaining why she is not improving.
quotations.analysis: The most important sentence in the story is delivered in a parenthesis, in a whisper, and immediately hedged with perhaps. She knows the cause, cannot say it aloud, and says it to paper — which is why the paper has to be dead before it is safe.

quotations.text: You see he does not believe I am sick!
quotations.context: After quoting the diagnosis her husband and brother agree on.
quotations.analysis: The exclamation mark is doing the work of an argument she is not allowed to make. Being disbelieved, not being ill, is the condition the story is about, and it is stated plainly on the first page and never taken seriously by anyone in the house.

quotations.text: If a physician of high standing, and one’s own husband, assures friends and relatives that there is really nothing the matter with one but temporary nervous depression—a slight hysterical tendency—what is one to do?
quotations.context: Explaining why her own account of herself carries no weight.
quotations.analysis: The shift to the impersonal 'one' is the sound of someone arguing in a register that might be listened to. The two roles — physician and husband — are stacked deliberately, because each is used to settle what the other cannot.

quotations.text: So I take phosphates or phosphites—whichever it is—and tonics, and journeys, and air, and exercise, and am absolutely forbidden to “work” until I am well again.
quotations.context: Listing the treatment.
quotations.analysis: The list runs on as though the items were equivalent, then arrives at the one that matters, with 'work' in quotation marks — his word, handed back. Her uncertainty about the medicine is comic; her certainty about the ban is not.

quotations.text: Personally, I believe that congenial work, with excitement and change, would do me good.
quotations.context: Her own view of what would help, offered once.
quotations.analysis: ‘Personally’ is the word of someone whose opinion rests on personality, not evidence. Her prescription is the opposite of his in every particular, and the story's ending is the demonstration that she was right.

quotations.text: John laughs at me, of course, but one expects that in marriage.
quotations.context: After admitting she believes the house is haunted.
quotations.analysis: Eleven words that describe a marriage and excuse it in the same breath. 'Of course' and 'one expects' are the story's method: the narrator supplies the defence before the reader can object, and the defence is the evidence.

quotations.text: He is very careful and loving, and hardly lets me stir without special direction.
quotations.context: Describing the daily regime.
quotations.analysis: Care and control are stated as one thing, because in this house they are. The sentence can be read as gratitude or as a description of custody, and the story never chooses — it simply keeps producing examples.

quotations.text: I don’t like our room a bit. I wanted one downstairs that opened on the piazza and had roses all over the window, and such pretty old-fashioned chintz hangings! but John would not hear of it.
quotations.context: On being given the top-floor nursery instead.
quotations.analysis: The only choice she asks to make in the whole story, and it is refused with a reason about windows and beds. Everything that follows happens because she is in this room and not that one.

quotations.text: The color is repellant, almost revolting; a smouldering, unclean yellow, strangely faded by the slow-turning sunlight.
quotations.context: Her first sustained description of the wallpaper.
quotations.analysis: This is expert writing, and the story knows it: rhythm, three adjectives that pull in different directions, and a last clause in which light itself becomes a stain. The woman who is not fit to hold a pen produces the best prose in the house.

quotations.text: It is dull enough to confuse the eye in following, pronounced enough to constantly irritate and provoke study
quotations.context: On the pattern itself.
quotations.analysis: A description of the paper and of her situation in one clause: dull enough to be maddening, marked enough to demand attention. 'Provoke study' is the giveaway — she has been forbidden intellectual work and has found some anyway.

quotations.text: There is a recurrent spot where the pattern lolls like a broken neck and two bulbous eyes stare at you upside-down.
quotations.context: Cataloguing the pattern's features.
quotations.analysis: The first body in the paper is a corpse, seen upside down and looking back. The observation is offered in the same matter-of-fact tone as the colour, which is how the story moves from decoration to horror without changing register.

quotations.text: But John says if I feel so I shall neglect proper self-control; so I take pains to control myself—before him, at least, and that makes me very tired.
quotations.context: After admitting she cries at nothing.
quotations.analysis: The performance of wellness is itself exhausting, and she is the only person who can see what it takes out of her. ‘Before him, at least’ announces that there are now two versions of her: the one in the room and the one in the journal.

quotations.text: at night in any kind of light, in twilight, candlelight, lamplight, and worst of all by moonlight, it becomes bars!
quotations.context: On what the sub-pattern looks like after dark.
quotations.analysis: Four kinds of light, listed in the order they fall on the wall, and then the word the room has been asking for. The bars are real — the windows have them — so the paper is not inventing the cage, only repeating it.

quotations.text: There are things in that paper that nobody knows but me, or ever will.
quotations.context: As her interest in the paper becomes private property.
quotations.analysis: Knowledge is the one thing the household has not taken, so she hoards it. The sentence is triumphant and also isolating, and from here on the story’s secrecy is her doing, not theirs.

quotations.text: The front pattern does move—and no wonder! The woman behind shakes it!
quotations.context: The moment the pattern is explained.
quotations.analysis: A design becomes an event: something is behind it and is trying to get out. 'No wonder' is the tone of a problem solved, which is why the sentence is frightening — she is not raving, she is concluding.

quotations.text: Sometimes I think there are a great many women behind, and sometimes only one, and she crawls around fast, and her crawling shakes it all over.
quotations.context: Watching the paper by daylight.
quotations.analysis: The figure multiplies and the story widens: one woman behind a pattern is a haunting, a great many is a social fact. The sentence is the closest the story comes to naming who else is in rooms like this.

quotations.text: I always lock the door when I creep by daylight.
quotations.context: Immediately after describing the woman creeping outside.
quotations.analysis: The two figures merge here, in a subordinate clause, without announcement. The narrator has begun doing what she has been describing, and the journal records it as a sensible precaution.

quotations.text: I am getting angry enough to do something desperate.
quotations.context: After John refuses again to leave the house early.
quotations.analysis: The word ‘angry’ arrives late and is followed by a plan, not a complaint. The story's last movement begins here: everything after this sentence is action.

quotations.text: Life is very much more exciting now than it used to be.
quotations.context: On the change in her days since the paper began to move.
quotations.analysis: She was told that excitement and change would harm her and has found both by herself, in a locked room, with a wall. The sentence is cheerful, and the cheerfulness is the most alarming thing in the story.

quotations.text: “I’ve got out at last,” said I, “in spite of you and Jane! And I’ve pulled off most of the paper, so you can’t put me back!”
quotations.context: Spoken to John through the door he has just opened.
quotations.analysis: The only speech she makes in the story, and the first sentence in it without a hedge. 'Jane' appears nowhere else: readers have taken it for her own name, for Jennie misprinted, and for the self she has just left behind. The victory and the disaster are the same act.

quotations.text: Now why should that man have fainted? But he did, and right across my path by the wall, so that I had to creep over him every time!
quotations.context: The last lines of the story.
quotations.analysis: The doctor is unconscious on the floor and the patient is still moving. Calling him 'that man' completes the reversal, and the mild puzzlement of the question is what makes the ending land: she has got past him, and does not much wonder why.

timeline.label: Charlotte Perkins born in Hartford
timeline.detail: Her father left the family early; she grew up moving between relatives, with an education she largely arranged herself.

timeline.label: Charlotte Perkins marries Charles Walter Stetson
timeline.detail: She had hesitated for two years, telling him she doubted she was fit for marriage.

timeline.label: Gilman's daughter Katharine born; depression follows
timeline.detail: The illness the story draws on began within weeks of the birth.

timeline.label: Gilman undergoes S. Weir Mitchell's rest cure
timeline.detail: Treated in Philadelphia by S. Weir Mitchell and sent home told to live as domestic a life as possible and never to touch pen, brush or pencil again.

timeline.label: Gilman leaves her marriage and moves to Pasadena
timeline.detail: Separation and a move to Pasadena, where she began to write and lecture; the divorce followed in 1894.

timeline.label: The Yellow Wall-Paper written
timeline.detail: Composed in June, in two days, and turned down by the Atlantic Monthly's editor, who said he could not forgive himself for making others as miserable as it had made him.

timeline.label: The Giant Wistaria printed
timeline.detail: Published in The New England Magazine in June, seven months before its companion piece.

timeline.label: The Yellow Wall-Paper printed
timeline.detail: In The New England Magazine for January, with illustrations; some readers wrote in to ask whether such a case could be real.

timeline.label: The first book edition
timeline.detail: Issued by Small, Maynard & Co. in Boston, the text behind most later American reprints.

timeline.label: Gilman's essay 'Why I Wrote The Yellow Wallpaper?'
timeline.detail: In her own magazine The Forerunner, Gilman said she had sent the story to Mitchell and heard that he had altered his treatment — an account no other source confirms.

timeline.label: Gilman dies in Pasadena
timeline.detail: Facing inoperable cancer, she ended her own life, having written that a last duty is to choose one's own way out.

timeline.label: The Feminist Press reprint
timeline.detail: Elaine Hedges's edition returned the story to print and to teaching, where it has stayed.

places.name: Providence, Rhode Island
places.note: Where she married, had her daughter, and first became ill.

places.name: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania
places.note: S. Weir Mitchell practised here; the rest cure she was sent for in 1887.

places.name: Pasadena, California
places.note: Where she wrote the story in June 1890, two years after leaving her marriage.

places.name: Boston, Massachusetts
places.note: The New England Magazine, which printed both stories, and Small, Maynard & Co., which first published the Wall-Paper as a book.

criticalViews.position: A case against the rest cure
criticalViews.summary: Gilman said in 1913 that she wrote it to reach Weir Mitchell and to keep other women out of his hands, and the story names him inside the fiction.
criticalViews.counter: Her account of Mitchell changing his practice has never been corroborated, and the story is far stranger than a protest needs to be — the pattern, the smell and the creeping women do no argumentative work at all.

criticalViews.position: A ghost story without a ghost
criticalViews.summary: Everything gothic is present: the ancestral hall, the locked room, the figure that appears at night, the last-page revelation.
criticalViews.counter: The supernatural is raised and dropped on the first page, and what remains is a medical arrangement everyone in the story finds reasonable. The horror is that no rule is broken.

criticalViews.summary: She gets out, the doctor faints, and the last sentence is hers — a reading that treats madness as the only available escape.
criticalViews.counter: She is creeping in a stripped room over a man who will wake up, and the tenancy ends that day. Whatever she has escaped, the house has not stopped being the place she is in.

essayQuestions.question: How does the journal form shape what the reader can know?
essayQuestions.focus: Narration, secrecy and the gaps between entries
plan: Establish the conditions of the writing: forbidden, hidden, done between visits, and exhausting to produce.
Show how the early entries hedge — perhaps, one expects, of course — and what those hedges tell us about the audience she imagines.
Use the gaps: the birth, the baby and the worst days are absent, so the silences carry information the sentences do not.
Track the change in tense and sentence length after the door is locked.
Conclude on the last speech, the only direct speech in the story, and what the reader has to accept in order to take it at face value.

essayQuestions.question: Is John a villain?
essayQuestions.focus: Authority, marriage and the ordinariness of harm
plan: Collect what he actually does: carries her upstairs, reads to her, schedules her hours, refuses the downstairs room, threatens Weir Mitchell.
Weigh the narrator's own testimony that he is careful and loving, and consider why the story has her supply it.
Set his laughter beside her exclamation that he does not believe she is sick, and examine the effect of putting them on the same page.
Consider the professional frame: two physicians and a specialist held in reserve, so that disagreement counts as symptom.
Close on the fainting: what kind of antagonist is disposed of by being stepped over?

essayQuestions.question: What is the wallpaper?
essayQuestions.focus: Symbol, reading and the work she is not allowed
plan: Begin with the paper as an object: colour, smell, torn patches, sub-pattern, the recurrent broken neck.
Show the narrator doing literary criticism on it — following the pattern, testing it in different lights, forming and revising a reading.
Trace the moment interpretation becomes identification, in the clause about locking the door when she creeps by daylight.
Ask what the bars owe to the real barred windows, and what that does to a symbolic reading.
Decide whether the paper is a mirror, a text or a prison, and whether the story lets you choose.

essayQuestions.question: Why print The Giant Wistaria alongside it?
essayQuestions.focus: Two silencings, told from inside and outside
plan: Summarise the second story: a daughter's disgrace, a family's departure, and a century of ignorance above her remains.
Compare the narrators: an unnamed woman writing in secret, and a party of tenants competing to invent a history.
Note what each story withholds — the Wall-Paper never explains the figure, the Wistaria never gives the woman a voice at all.
Consider the effect of reading them in publication order, the ghost story first.
Argue for what the pairing adds that either story alone does not.

discussionQuestions: The narrator is never named. Does the last line give her one?
She writes that John is careful and loving. Do you believe her?
At what point in the story does she stop being a reliable witness — and does the marriage stop being accurately described at the same moment?
The room was a nursery, with a gate and rings in the wall. What else could it have been?
Is the ending a breakdown, an escape, or a refusal to choose between them?
Gilman said she wrote the story to change a doctor's mind. Does knowing that make it a better or a smaller thing?

related.why: The other great story of the 1890s told by a narrator you cannot check, published six years later.
Kate Chopin's 1899 novel of a woman's rebellion inside marriage, met with the same critical discomfort.
A wife managed by a husband who calls her his little creature, and the door she closes at the end of it.
The madwoman upstairs, seen from the other side of the ceiling.
Septimus and his doctors: the rest cure thirty years on, and the same proportion of care to control.
